# Case: Uber ATG automated test vehicle (Tempe, Arizona, 2018)

Source: NTSB Highway Accident Report HAR-19/03. This is a description of the system and its use before the crash. It does not include the investigation findings.

## System
A modified Volvo XC90 SUV is used by Uber Advanced Technologies Group (ATG) to test an automated driving system (ADS) on public roads. The ADS is designed to drive the vehicle without human input in defined conditions, up to about 45 mph in this test program.

## Main parts
- Sensors: roof-mounted lidar, radar units and cameras covering the area around the vehicle.
- Perception: detects objects around the vehicle, classifies each one (for example vehicle, pedestrian, bicycle, other), and tracks it over time.
- Prediction: estimates where each tracked object will go next, using its class and recent movement.
- Planning and control: chooses a path and speed, and controls steering, throttle and braking.
- Vehicle: the Volvo factory driver-assistance features (such as forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking) are part of the base vehicle.

## People
- One vehicle operator sits in the driver seat. The operator is responsible for watching the road and taking over control when needed. The operator also uses a tablet-style interface to tag events and check system status.
- Other road users share the road: pedestrians, cyclists and other drivers. They are not aware of the test program.

## Operating context
Public multi-lane roads in an urban area, day and night, with posted speed limits, marked crosswalks, intersections and street lighting that varies by location.

requirements.text: The system shall fuse lidar, radar, and camera data so that any pedestrian occluded in a single sensor’s view is still detected, and shall raise a detection‑confidence alert if line‑of‑sight blockage is identified.

The system shall achieve at least 95 % classification accuracy for dynamic objects (pedestrians, cyclists) in urban scenarios, and shall treat any object with a ≥10 % probability of being a pedestrian as a collision hazard.

The prediction module shall output updated trajectories for all detected dynamic objects within 100 ms of the latest sensor update, ensuring the planner receives predictions before the next control cycle.

The vehicle operator shall maintain visual attention on the forward roadway at least 95 % of the time while the ADS is engaged, and the system shall issue an alert if gaze is away for more than 2 seconds.
The ADS shall provide a clear takeover request signal and shall not accept manual steering, throttle, or brake inputs until it has completed a safe stop or signaled inability to maintain safety.

The planner shall consider any detected pedestrian or any area designated as a crosswalk as a potential crossing zone, and shall never generate a path that traverses a crosswalk while a pedestrian is present, regardless of traffic‑signal status.

The control module shall automatically apply braking to maintain a minimum safety distance of at least 2 seconds time‑to‑collision to any crossing pedestrian, and shall verify that the braking command is executed within 50 ms of the planner’s request.

The speed‑planning component shall continuously evaluate time‑to‑stop against distance to the nearest obstacle and shall reduce speed at least 2 seconds before a projected collision point to guarantee sufficient stopping distance.

The system shall receive and integrate real‑time map and infrastructure updates (e.g., construction zones, lane closures) at a minimum frequency of 1 Hz, and shall flag any loss of map data for more than 5 seconds as a degraded‑operation condition.

The perception subsystem shall employ high‑dynamic‑range imaging and adaptive exposure control so that camera images retain sufficient contrast for reliable object classification under direct sunlight glare, maintaining a classification confidence of ≥0.8.
